title: 2007 was particularly good year for aviation safety
text:
Statistics supplied by a survey from the Geneva-based Aircraft Crashes Record Office (ACRO) and by aviation insurance specialist Aon suggest that 2007 was an unusually good year for safety in the aviation industry. The ACRO reports that fatal aircraft accidents involving planes carrying over six people were at their lowest since 1963, while Aon reports that fatal accidents on commercial airliners totaled 23, which Flight International reports to be an all-time low.
ACRO reports that 136 crashes killed a total of 965 people worldwide. It says this is 28 fewer crashes than 2006, and also a 25% decrease in fatalities. Flight reported that 23 fatal commercial airliner crashes killed a total of 597 people. That accident rate is the lowest it has ever been, and both figures are well below the average for the last decade, which came in at 35.5 and 846.3 respectively. In 2006, 27 fatal commercial aviation accidents killed 863 people.
"In 2007, more than two billion were traveling worldwide and we have thousands and thousands of aircraft, airplanes flying every day worldwide, it means that airplanes, aviation is one of the safest transport modes in the world," said Ronan Hubert, aviation accident historian and head of ACRO.
According to Hubert, the highest number of accidents recorded in an individual country was 34 in the United States, followed by Canada, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Colombia and Indonesia. He went on to criticise African air safety, blaming political factors: civil war in Somalia, corruption and the Darfur problem in Sudan, and corruption in the DRC.
The worst aviation disaster all year was the crash of TAM Linhas Aereas Flight 3054 in Brazil, killing 187 on board and 12 on the ground. Congo saw more fatal commercial air crashes than any other country. Indonesia also had a particularly poor year, with two major disasters.

title: GSK rejects three Unilever bids to buy consumer healthcare arm, says unit was "fundamentally undervalued"
text:
United Kingdom-based pharmaceutical giant GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) confirmed January 15 it had rejected three "unsolicited, conditional and non-binding proposals" by Unilever to acquire its Consumer Healthcare division, including one bid of GBP50 billion in value made on December 20, believing Unilever "fundamentally undervalued" the business and its potential.
News that Unilever attempted to buy GSK Consumer Healthcare for 50 billion pounds was first reported by The Sunday Times, and subsequently confirmed by both companies. Had the acquisition gone through, it would have been the largest deal since the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic, and one of the biggest ever among companies listed on the London Stock Exchange.
A brief response on the Unilever website confirmed it "had approached GSK and Pfizer about a potential acquisition", and added that GSK Consumer Healthcare "would be a strong strategic fit" as the company looks to rework its portfolio. GSK indicated the proposals were "carefully evaluated" by its board of directors, but unanimously rejected under the conclusion they "were not in the best interests of GSK shareholders" and "failed to reflect the intrinsic value of the business and its potential."
The BBC's business editor Simon Jack wrote that a standard takeover premium would be about 30%. GSK said it remains focused on executing its proposed demerger of the Consumer Healthcare business, on track to be achieved in mid-2022. Unilever later said it would not raise its offer above GBP50 billion, citing financial discipline for shareholders.

title: 'Stop being so damn respectful' say free speech supporters in London
text:
Atheists, secularists, and supporters of free speech rallied in London today to protest what they feel is an "increased confidence of Islamists to censor free expression publicly". Around 200 people gathered on the steps of the memorial to King George V in Old Palace Yard opposite the House of Lords in Westminster.
Anne Marie Waters from the 'One Law for All' group, which protests against sharia law in the United Kingdom, said that freedom of expression was "the greatest freedom we have" and included "the freedom to offend". Accusations of Islamophobia against those who reposted the Jesus and Mo webcomic was one of a number of incidents highlighted by speakers.
Susan Zhuang from the University College London Atheist, Secularist and Humanist society spoke of the reaction to the posting of the cartoon to their Facebook profile, saying they were naive but never expected the backlash that followed.
Philosopher A.C. Grayling spoke at the rally. Richard Dawkins argued that people should "stop being so damn respectful". Without freedom of speech, Dawkins said, society would be in a "scientific, technological, moral dark age".

title: Grey Wolves are Still Protected by the Endangered Species Act
text:
A federal judge has ruled that grey wolves in the western United States remain protected under the Endangered Species Act, blocking a Trump-era rule that had removed federal protections for the species across most of the country.
The ruling restores Endangered Species Act protections to wolf populations in several states, reversing a 2020 decision by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that delisted the species. Conservation groups had sued, arguing the delisting was premature and that wolf populations had not sufficiently recovered or were not secure from renewed hunting pressure in several states.
Wildlife officials and ranching groups have pushed back, arguing that wolf populations have rebounded enough in some regions to be managed at the state level, and that continued federal protection imposes unnecessary restrictions on ranchers and hunters. Conservationists welcomed the ruling, saying state-level management plans in some states would have allowed aggressive hunting and trapping that could undo decades of recovery efforts. The Fish and Wildlife Service said it was reviewing the decision.

title: UK defers junk food deals, advertisement restrictions
text:
The United Kingdom Department of Health and Social Care on Friday postponed restrictions on multibuy promotional deals and online and TV advertising for junk food products by one year.
The deferral affects a ban on deals incentivising multiple purchases of foods high in fat, salt or sugar, including buy one, get one free and complimentary refills for soft drinks, and on paid TV advertisements before 9pm and online. A Department press release attributes the delay to the "unprecedented global economic situation", and states that it is hoped postponing restrictions will give businesses "more time to prepare for the restrictions on advertising".
The Independent wrote of backbench Conservative MPs having reportedly criticised the deal as evidence of a "nanny state". The Food and Drink Federation said the delay "makes sense" in response to "high inflation", though the Children's Food Campaign argues multibuy deals do not save consumers money, but instead increase junk food purchases.
Campaigner and chef Jamie Oliver called it "a wasted opportunity" that "starts to erode the whole obesity strategy". He urged "real leadership" from Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Public Health Minister Maggie Throup said "we're committed to doing everything we can to help people live healthier lives", while her Labour counterpart Andrew Gwynne called it a reversal.

title: Musique Libre Femmes plays for Women's History Month at Tompkins Square Library in New York City
text:
Musique Libre Femmes, an all-women free jazz ensemble featuring Cheryl Pyle on flute, Mary Cherney on flute, Jeong Lim Yang on bass, and Yuko Togami on drums, performed at Tompkins Square Library in New York City as part of programming for Women's History Month.
The performance was organized as part of the "Lady Got Chops" festival, a recurring celebration of women improvisers in the free jazz and experimental music scenes. The ensemble's improvisational style draws on extended technique and free interplay among the musicians rather than fixed compositions.
The event highlighted the contributions of women to a genre, free jazz, that has historically been dominated by male performers, and was one of a number of similar programs at branch libraries across the city during March in honor of Women's History Month.

title: The Ancient Pyramids of the World, a new photo exhibition by Viktor Pinchuk took place in Crimea
text:
An exhibition of works by Russian photographer Viktor Pinchuk was held at the Genoese Fortress Museum-Reserve in Sudak. It was timed to coincide with the annual "Night of Geography" event of the Russian Geographical Society.
The exhibition was held in a digital format, which allowed an increase in the number of works on display without transporting them to the exhibition. The author, who traveled to dozens of countries in Africa, Asia, Oceania and Latin America, presented to the audience a collection of photographs taken at different times, all united by one theme. The exhibition is called The Ancient Pyramids of the World. It contains images of archaeological monuments from Egypt, Sudan, Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Indonesia, Cambodia, Samoa and Peru.
The author highlighted the once pyramid-shaped and now almost completely destroyed Pulemelei Mound, located in the impenetrable jungle of the Samoan island of Savai'i, which is practically unknown outside a narrow circle of professional archaeologists. What visitors learned, according to the author, should encourage them to pay more attention to the study of historical and geographical objects of the planet.

title: Spider-Man to save Obama's Inauguration Day in upcoming Marvel comic
text:
A six-page tongue-in-cheek story, to appear in The Amazing Spider-Man issue 583, "Spidey Meets the President!" is created by Zeb Wells, Todd Nauck and Frank D'Armata. The issue features Peter Parker visiting Washington, D.C., on photo assignment for the Daily Bugle, covering President-elect Obama's inauguration, when an imposter -- the supervillain Chameleon -- tries to take Obama's place.
The issue's cover will feature Obama smiling, with a thumbs up pose. Spider-Man is featured hanging upside-down beside him, whispering: "Hey, if you get to be on my cover, can I be on the dollar bill?" The issue is not official merchandise of the US Democratic Party, Obama campaign, the Obama-Biden Transition Project, or White House.
According to Marvel comic's editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, the publication learned that the President-elect is a long-time fan and collector as a kid of the Marvel super hero. "When we heard that president-elect Obama is a collector of Spider-Man comics, we knew that these two historic figures had to meet in our comics' Marvel Universe," Quesada said. During his campaigning, Mr. Obama made mention of Spider-Man at child-oriented events.

title: Archaeologists uncover Britain's earliest known hospital
text:
Archaeologists from the University of Winchester in Hampshire, England have discovered what they believe to be the earliest known hospital in the United Kingdom. Radiocarbon dating of burials at the former leper hospital of St Mary Magdalen in Winchester returned results ranging from 960-1030 A.D., centuries earlier than the hospital's previously assumed founding date of 1170.
Archaeologists also found artefacts, postholes, and foundations that date to the same period, including what appears to be a large sunken structure underneath a medieval infirmary. Many of the bodies from the site dating to the 10th and early 11th century show signs of advanced leprosy.
Before this excavation, most historians and archaeologists thought hospitals in Britain only dated from after the Norman conquest of 1066. "This is an important archaeological development," said Dr Simon Roffey of the University of Winchester, which conducted the dig. "Historically, it has always been assumed that hospitals were a post-conquest phenomena."

title: Mascots for Vancouver 2010 Olympics based on native mythology
text:
The Vancouver Organizing Committee unveiled the official mascots for the 2010 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games, drawing on First Nations mythology from British Columbia for inspiration. The mascots -- Miga, Quatchi, and Sumi -- represent a sea bear, a sasquatch, and an animal guardian spirit respectively, while a fourth figure, Mukmuk, serves as a sidekick mascot.
Miga is described as a young sea bear who lives in the ocean, drawing on legends of an orca that transforms into a bear. Quatchi is a young sasquatch, inspired by legends of the elusive creature said to roam the forests of British Columbia. Sumi is an animal spirit who wears the hat of the Thunderbird and the boots of the black bear, with wings like an orca's tail.
Organizers said the designs were intended to celebrate the indigenous heritage of the host region and connect the Games to local legend. The mascots became part of a wide range of licensed Olympic merchandise leading up to the Games.

title: Sandra Fluke gives keynote speech at Nebraska women's health event
text:
Women's rights advocate and Georgetown University Law Center graduate Sandra Fluke delivered the keynote address at Planned Parenthood's annual fundraiser in Lincoln, Nebraska on Tuesday, December 4, her first visit to the state.
Fluke rose to national attention in February 2012 after being denied the opportunity to speak at a Republican-led House hearing on insurance coverage for birth control, and was later the target of on-air insults from radio host Rush Limbaugh, who called her derogatory names. The remarks sparked national debate and drew a phone call of support from President Barack Obama.
Asked ahead of the speech whether she planned to address the controversy directly, Fluke said she would mainly focus on women's health care rather than rehashing the personal attacks. "It certainly has been a different 2012 than the one I expected, for better and worse," Fluke said. She said her goal was "giving a voice to people who don't always have one," and that she planned to continue speaking out on reproductive health policy regardless of the criticism she had faced.

title: John Reed on Orwell, God, self-destruction and the future of writing
text:
Novelist John Reed, known for Snowball's Chance, a controversial send-up of George Orwell's Animal Farm, sat down with Wikinews to discuss religion, self-destructive creativity, and where narrative form is headed next.
On faith, Reed described himself as somewhere within a loosely Gnostic Christian framework, while saying he could not abide a religion that would distinguish a child from its parents based on lineage, calling that kind of distinction "sinister and destructive."
Asked about why so many talented writers and artists seem driven to sabotage their own work, Reed reflected on friends from his early career who were "hell-bent on self-destruction," describing a novelist who endlessly rewrote a finished manuscript until it was ruined. "The inclination to be a creative person is to blow things up," he said.
Looking ahead, Reed predicted new narrative forms being born -- Biblical epics played out across both print and electronic mediums -- as old structures are taken and made new again, a theme he said runs through both his fiction and his worldview.

title: New Jersey real estate investor charged with $2 million theft
text:
The owner of a New Jersey real estate investment firm has been charged with using $2 million of his company's money for construction at his home and other projects not related to work.
Gary Klein, owner of the Asbury Park-based REI Group Inc., surrendered himself to police after a Monmouth County grand jury indicted him on one count of theft by deception. The charges were the result of a three-year investigation into his practices.
Klein, 45, of Colts Neck Township, faces up to 10 years in state prison if convicted. He was released Friday after posting $75,000 bail. Klein attracted clients by telling them he would invest their money in projects that would result in returns of 12 to 85 percent, and prosecutors said his actions mirrored those of a Ponzi scheme. Robert Weir, Klein's attorney, said the operation was not a Ponzi scheme, but legitimate business investments that went bad as the economy declined.

title: Police called to investigate after tenant draws swastikas in landlord's house
text:
Police were called to a rental property after a landlord discovered that an outgoing tenant had drawn multiple swastikas on the interior walls of the home before moving out.
The landlord said he discovered the symbols while inspecting the property after the tenant vacated, and reported the damage to local police as a possible hate-motivated vandalism incident. Officers attended the scene to document the damage and begin an investigation into who was responsible and whether charges would be pursued under vandalism or hate-crime statutes.
The former tenant has not been publicly identified pending the outcome of the investigation. The landlord said he was left to repaint the affected rooms before the property could be re-let, and that he intended to pursue the cost of repairs through the tenant's security deposit and, if necessary, small claims court.

title: Rescue underway for teen solo sailor
text:
A rescue operation is underway after sixteen-year-old American Abby Sunderland, attempting to sail around the world by herself, lost contact with her family while in the Indian Ocean.
Sunderland, from Thousand Oaks, California, had originally hoped to become the youngest person to sail around the world nonstop by herself. She departed from Marina del Rey, California on January 23, 2010 and was about halfway through the attempt when her family lost communication with her Thursday morning. That night, an Australian plane was able to locate her 40-foot boat, Wild Eyes, which had lost its mast earlier.
Sunderland had been sailing amid a rough storm in the Indian Ocean early Thursday when her boat was flipped over and the mast broke off. After losing contact, the teenager activated two manual distress radiobeacons, or EPIRBs, and a search-and-rescue operation was formed. Sunderland's family has been criticized for allowing her to depart the United States at the beginning of the year, because she would likely arrive in the Indian Ocean during the region's winter. Her brother Zac had completed a circumnavigation at age seventeen the year before.

title: Japanese adults rank high in literacy and numeracy in OECD survey
text:
Compared to other countries surveyed, Japan ranks as one of the best-performing surveyed countries in both literacy and numeracy, according to the OECD's Survey of Adult Skills. Internationally, Japan ranks first amongst surveyed countries for literacy proficiency amongst adults.
The correlation between individual performance on numeracy and literacy tests in Japan is 0.846, slightly below the surveyed average of 0.867. In proficiency at problem solving, Japan finishes tenth amongst surveyed nations. Adults were allowed to opt out of using computers for this test, and Japan had the third largest percentage at 15.9% opting to do so.
The Japanese data said adult literacy skills did not impact on social inequality, and that literacy is not a barrier to social mobility, in contrast to countries like the United States where literacy skills correlate strongly to social mobility. The percentage of adults who have completed university in Japan is above the global average, particularly for people aged 25 to 34 years, and Japan is below the global average for adults who have not finished high school.

title: Researchers identify genetic link to peanut allergies
text:
An international research team at Dundee University in Scotland has established that a gene called Filaggrin is linked to peanut allergies. Calling the research a "potential breakthrough", the team says it is the first firm evidence of a genetic element to the potentially fatal condition.
The team, including scientists from the Netherlands, the UK, Ireland, and Canada, had previously identified Filaggrin as linked to eczema and asthma. The gene is involved in ensuring the skin is an effective barrier to irritants, and Dundee University fellow Dr. Sara Brown described investigating peanut allergy linkage as a "logical next step."
The university says that in the last two to three decades there has been a major rise in peanut allergies, which now affect 1-2% of young Britons. The gene is a factor in around 20% of the cases studied. Dundee's Professor Irwin McLean, a Filaggrin expert, said more work is required to fully understand the causes of the disease. "What we have now shown is that the Filaggrin defect is there for people who have peanut allergy but who don't have eczema, which shows a clear link between Filaggrin and peanut allergy," he explained.

title: Japanese researchers create smell sensor using genetically engineered frog eggs
text:
A University of Tokyo group of researchers, led by bioengineer Shoji Takeuchi, have made an electronic sensor capable of smelling gases using genetically engineered frog cells. Since previous sensors based on quartz rods were not very accurate, the scientist decided to try a biological approach instead.
Previous smell sensors were based on quartz rods, which vibrate when a substance binds to them, but gases are distinguished by their molar masses, which can be similar for molecules with different structure, relatively often triggering a false positive. Trying to find a more accurate solution, Takeuchi followed an example from the insect world: "when you think about the mosquito, it is able to find people because of carbon dioxide from the human. So the mosquito has CO2 receptors. When we can extract DNA from the mosquito we can put this DNA into the frog eggs to detect CO2."
Takeuchi says the frog eggs are very practical for genetic engineering and can be conveniently used to develop smell sensors for a wide range of gases. "We believe that a shared ability to smell might open a new relationship between man and robot," he said, noting potential uses identifying body odors, detecting air or water pollution, and food safety monitoring.

title: Largest exoplanet so far is discovered
text:
The largest extrasolar planet or exoplanet has been discovered orbiting the star GSC 02620-00648, around 1,435 light years away. The planet, named TrES-4, after the Transatlantic Exoplanet Survey (TrES), is 1.7 times the size of the planet Jupiter.
TrES-4 also has a lower mass than Jupiter and an extremely low density of 0.2 grams per cubic centimetre, less than a wine cork. Georgi Mandushev of the Lowell Observatory in Arizona said, "It's way lower than the density of water." TrES-4 orbits its star at a distance of only 7 million km, meaning the temperature of the planet is estimated at 1,327 degrees Celsius.
Mandushev went on to say, "Because of the planet's relatively weak pull on its upper atmosphere, some of the atmosphere probably escapes in a comet-like tail." The discovery was made using a network of automated telescopes and detected as the planet passed in front of, or "transited," its parent star, the only planet-finding method that currently allows scientists to calculate a planet's size directly.

title: Largest mass extinction in 65 million years underway, scientists say
text:
Environmental scientists say they have concrete evidence that the planet is undergoing the "largest mass extinction in 65 million years". Leading environmental scientist Professor Norman Myers says the Earth is experiencing its "Sixth Extinction." Scientists forecast that up to five million species will be lost this century.
"We are well into the opening phase of a mass extinction of species. There are about 10 million species on earth. If we carry on as we are, we could lose half of all those 10 million species," Myers said. If more is not done, Myers says, the planet will continue to lose around 50 species per day compared to the natural extinction rate of one species every five years.
He projected this rate in the late 1980s to much criticism, but the figure is now widely accepted by scientists. "The whole thing is taking place in what you might call a flickering of an evolutionary eye," said Myers. Recent research has also suggested that climate change may be driving widespread frog and amphibian extinctions through its effect on a fatal skin fungus.

title: British surfers catch more than waves: Scientists find antibiotic-resistant bacteria
text:
In findings published Sunday in Environment International, a team from Britain's University of Exeter reports that surfers and bodyboarders are roughly three times as likely to carry antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli and other bacteria, compared to other people who recreate in the coastal waters of the United Kingdom.
The epidemiological study, nicknamed the "Beach Bum Survey", was performed on 143 regular surfers and bodyboarders and a control group of 130 non-surfing friends of similar age and sex. The antibiotic failed to kill the bacteria in about 9% (13 out of 143) of surfer samples, compared to 3% of the samples from the control group. Bacteria from surfers were also four times as likely to possess genes transferable between bacterial strains, which can help antibiotic-susceptible bacteria become resistant.
David Smith of Surfers Against Sewage, which helped organise the volunteers, said the study was not meant to discourage surfing: "Water quality in the UK has improved vastly in the past 30 years and is some of the cleanest in Europe. Recognising coastal waters as a pathway for antibiotic resistance can allow policy makers to make changes to protect water users." Previous studies have shown surfers swallow roughly ten times as much seawater as swimmers.

title: Brazil defends China against human rights violation charges in UN
text:
Brazil's Human Rights Secretary Nilmario Miranda said that Brazil will defend China in the United Nations Commission on Human Rights. According to him, the Chinese government showed some advances in the human rights area recently.
Last year Brazil voted for China and helped to stop a discussion on the subject in the UN. The only Latin American countries who favored China in the vote were Brazil and Cuba.
